## CHAPTER 17
TRIBUNALS, ADR AND LEGAL AID
THEME ANALYSIS PYQ pattern for this chapter
1. REPEATS

#### A. Constitutional Basis of Tribunals
- Articles 323A and 323B were inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 [2009]
- Article 323A: Parliament alone, and only for recruitment and service matters of public servants; Article 323B:
Parliament or a State legislature, for a listed set of subjects
- Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985; the Central Administrative Tribunal began on 1 November 1985 under Rajiv
Gandhi, not Lal Bahadur Shastri [2009]
- Members are drawn from both the judicial and the administrative streams [2009]
- L. Chandra Kumar (1997): review under Articles 226, 227 and 32 is Basic Structure, so tribunal orders stay
reviewable by a Division Bench of the High Court

#### B. Lok Adalats
- Statutory footing in Chapter VI of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 [2009, 2010]
- Takes both pending and pre litigation matters, and civil as well as criminal ones, the only bar being non
compoundable offences [2010]
- The award is deemed a decree of a civil court and no appeal lies against it [2009]
- Matrimonial and family disputes are regularly taken up, which is the standard distractor [2009]
- A bench is not composed of judicial officers alone; Permanent Lok Adalats cover public utility services up to Rs 1
crore and may decide on merits [2010]

#### C. Gram Nyayalayas
- Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, in force from 2 October 2009, one for every intermediate level Panchayat
- Presided over by a Nyayadhikari with the status, salary and powers of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class,
appointed by the State in consultation with the High Court
- A mobile court that sits in villages, with both civil and criminal jurisdiction, so the claim that it hears only civil cases is
wrong [2016]
- Not bound by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and local social activists may serve as conciliators [2016]

#### D. Legal Aid and the Legal Services Authorities
- Article 39A, a Directive Principle inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, is the source of free legal aid [2013,
2020]
- NALSA under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, with the Chief Justice of India as Patron in Chief, issues
guidelines to the State authorities [2013]
- The tiers: State Legal Services Authority under the Chief Justice of the High Court, District authority under the
District Judge, and a Taluk committee below it
- Section 12 entitlement list: SCs and STs, victims of trafficking or begar, women and children, persons with mental
illness or disability, industrial workmen and persons in custody [2020]
- The income ceiling and the transgender and senior citizen options are the recurring trap [2020]
- Also tested: Zero FIR under the BNSS [2026]
2. HOW THE FORMAT HAS CHANGED
- 2009 to 2016: two statement sets on CAT, Lok Adalats, NALSA and Gram Nyayalayas [2009, 2010, 2013, 2016]
- 2020: an eligibility code set on free legal aid [2020]
- 2026: three statements on Zero FIR under the BNSS [2026]
3. WHAT IS BEING ASKED NOW
- The new criminal law codes: Zero FIR [2026]
- Who qualifies for free legal aid [2020]

Tribunals[PRELIMS 2009]
1. Articles 323A and 323B were inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
2. Article 323A enables Parliament alone to provide for administrative tribunals for disputes relating to recruitment and
conditions of service of public servants of the Union and the States;
3. Article 323B lets Parliament or a State legislature set up tribunals for other matters: taxation, foreign exchange,
industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, elections, essential goods, urban property ceilings.
Under Article 323A, the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was enacted, and the CAT began work on 1 November
1985, under PM Rajiv Gandhi (not Lal Bahadur Shastri).
4. Its members are drawn from both the judicial and the administrative streams.
5. In L. Chandra Kumar (1997) the Supreme Court held that judicial review by the High Courts under Articles 226/227 and
by the Supreme Court under Article 32 is part of the Basic Structure, so tribunal decisions are subject to review by a
Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
6. Orders of the Central Administrative Tribunal and other tribunals are amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court
within whose territorial jurisdiction the tribunal is situated (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997);
7. a High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227 extends over all tribunals in its territory, except military
tribunals.
Lok Adalats[PRELIMS 2010,2009]
1. Given statutory status by Chapter VI (Sections 19-22) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
2. A Lok Adalat may take up both (i) a case pending before a court and (ii) a matter at the pre-litigation stage falling within
the jurisdiction of that court - so it is not confined to either.
3. It may settle civil as well as criminal matters, the only bar being offences that are non-compoundable under any law;
4. matrimonial and family disputes are regularly taken up.
5. Its award is deemed to be a decree of a civil court, is final and binding on all parties, and no appeal lies against it before
any court.
6. A bench is not composed only of judicial officers - it typically has a serving or retired judicial officer together with a
lawyer and a social worker.
7. National Lok Adalats are held on a single day across all courts in the country.
8. Permanent Lok Adalats under Section 22B deal with disputes relating to public utility services (transport, postal,
telegraph, power, water supply, insurance, hospitals, sanitation, etc.), with pecuniary jurisdiction up to Rs 1 crore;
9. uniquely, if conciliation fails they may decide the dispute on merits, but they cannot try an offence.
Gram Nyayalayas[PRELIMS 2016]
1. The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 (in force from 2 October 2009) provides for a Gram Nyayalaya for every Panchayat at
the intermediate level, or a group of contiguous intermediate-level Panchayats, with its headquarters at the intermediate
Panchayat headquarters.
2. It is presided over by a Nyayadhikari appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court, who has
the same status, salary and powers as a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
3. It is conceived as a mobile court: the Nyayadhikari periodically visits villages and disposes of cases at places other than
its headquarters.

---

### [Prelims Source Page 136](pages/prelims/prelims_page_136.pdf)

4. It exercises both civil and criminal jurisdiction over matters listed in the First and Second Schedules (criminal cases
being tried by summary procedure), so it is wrong to say it hears only civil cases.
5. It is not bound by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and is guided by the principles of natural justice, and it must endeavour
to settle disputes by conciliation through conciliators appointed for that purpose, which permits the use of local social
activists as mediators/conciliators.
Legal Aid & Legal Services Authorities[PRELIMS 2020,2013]
1. Article 39A (DPSP, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976) obliges the State to secure that the operation of the
legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied
justice by reason of economic or other disability.
2. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (brought into force 9 November 1995) constituted NALSA, with the Chief
Justice of India as Patron-in-Chief and a serving Supreme Court judge nominated by the President as Executive
Chairman;
3. the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee handles matters before the Supreme Court.
4. NALSA lays down policies and issues guidelines and directions to the State Legal Services Authorities for
implementing legal aid programmes and schemes throughout the country and disburses funds to them.
5. Section 12 entitles the following to free and competent legal services: members of SCs and STs;
6. victims of trafficking in human beings or begar (Article 23);
7. women and children;
8. persons with mental illness or disability;
9. victims of mass disaster, ethnic or caste violence, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster;
10. industrial workmen;
11. persons in custody (including in a protective home, juvenile home or psychiatric hospital); and persons whose annual
income is below the ceiling prescribed by the State Government (Rs 5,00,000 for cases before the Supreme Court;
commonly Rs 3,00,000 in most States, lower in some).
12. Entitlement is thus not automatic for all senior citizens or for all members of a backward class - an income test applies.
13. The State Legal Services Authority is headed by the Chief Justice of the High Court as Patron-in-Chief, with a serving
or retired High Court judge as Executive Chairman nominated by the Governor in consultation with the Chief Justice.
14. Every High Court also has a High Court Legal Services Committee for cases before it.
15. District Legal Services Authority in every district, chaired by the District Judge, and a Taluk (Sub-divisional) Legal
Services Committee headed by a senior civil judge, deliver legal aid and organise Lok Adalats at the grassroots.

3. Speedy Dispute Resolution: Eg. The NCLT is mandated to resolve corporate insolvency cases within a
strict 180-270 day window.
4. Cost-Effective Justice: Lower court fees and simplified filing make them accessible for individuals and

5. Accessibility: Eg. The NGT has five zonal benches (Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai, and Delhi) to ensure
regional coverage.
6. Flexibility and Informality: They follow the "Principles of Natural Justice" rather than the rigid
Evidence Act, ensuring fairness.
7. Alternative to Writ Jurisdiction: They act as the "court of first instance" for specialized matters, as per
the L. Chandra Kumar (1997) ruling.
8. Sector-Specific Regulation: They help in the smooth functioning of core sectors like Telecom,
Electricity, and Real Estate.
9. Insolvency & Bankruptcy Success: Tribunals have revolutionized debt recovery through the IBC 2016
framework. Eg. Recoveries through NCLT have surpassed ₹3 lakh crore.
Issues:
1. Lack of Independence: Tribunals are under the administrative control of the Line Ministry
2. High Pendency Rates:tribunals have over 5 lakh cases pending

Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021
- Abolition of 9 Appellate Tribunals, transferring their cases directly to the High Courts.
- It set the term of office for chairpersons and members at 4 years.
- It mandated that a person must be at least 50 years old to be appointed.
- Search-cum-Selection Committee headed by the CJI (or a nominee) with a "casting vote" to
recommend two names per vacancy, giving the executive the final choice.
- Mandated appointments within three months of the committee's recommendation.

1. Tribunal Reforms Act Case (Nov 2025): The SC struck down several sections of the 2021 Act as
unconstitutional. It struck down
a. Minimum age requirement of 50 years

Contempt of Court
Contempt of court refers to any act that disrespects or challenges the authority, integrity, or dignity of a
court. It includes defying court orders, witness tampering, withdrawing evidence, or non-compliance with
judicial requests.
Key Facts and Provisions
1. Article 129 empowers the Supreme Court as a Court of Record with the authority to punish for
contempt; Article 215 grants similar powers to High Courts.
2. Article 19(2): Includes "Contempt of Court" as a reasonable restriction.
3. Contempt of Courts Act, 1971: Provides the statutory framework, defining types of contempt,
procedures, and punishments.
4. Contempt of Court (Amendment) Act, 2006: Introduced "Truth" as a valid defense if it is in the public
interest and made bona fide.
5. Civil Contempt - Willful disobedience of a court's judgment, decree, order, or direction, or breach of an
undertaking given to the court.
6. Criminal Contempt - Includes publications or acts that:
a. Scandalize the court or lower its authority.
b. Interfere with judicial proceedings or obstruct justice.
c. Obstructs the administration of justice in any other manner.
7. Punishment - Up to six months of simple imprisonment, or a fine up to ₹2,000, or both.

Court Cases:
1. Prashant Bhushan Case(2020): The SC held that tweets criticizing the CJI "scandalized the court" and
undermined the dignity of the institution
2. Shanmugam @ Lakshminarayanan v. Madras HC (2025): contempt powers are meant to protect the
administration of justice, not to shield judges from individual criticism
3. Justice C.S. Karnan Case (2017): The first time a sitting High Court judge was sentenced to
imprisonment for contempt
4. M.V. Jayarajan vs. High Court of Kerala (2015) - the SC held that using abusive language in public
speeches while criticizing a court amounts to criminal contempt.
Need:
1. Ensuring Compliance: ensures court orders are not ignored by the executive or powerful private entities.
Eg. Civil contempt is used to enforce maintenance payments in matrimonial disputes.
2. Deterrence Against Perjury: Discourages parties from filing false affidavits or fabricated evidence. Eg.
criminal contempt for submitting forged land records in property suits.
3. Protecting Witnesses: Contempt powers are used to punish those who threaten witnesses in
high-profile criminal trials like the Lakhimpur Kheri case.
4. Maintaining Courtroom Decorum: Allows judges to manage disruptive behavior during hearings to
ensure an orderly trial process.
5. Curbing "Media Trials": Prevents sensationalist reporting from prejudicing the mind of the judge or the
public during active trials.
6. Safeguarding Judicial Independence: Protects judges from malicious political attacks intended to
influence their decision-making process.
7. Preventing Procedural Obstruction: Punishes officers who intentionally delay implementation of
time-bound judicial directives. Eg. Contempt petitions against Chief Secretaries
8. Upholding Public Confidence: Eg. in Arundhati Roy case, the SC found her in contempt for statements
that were perceived to erode public confidence in the judiciary
9. Protection of Subordinate Courts - the Act empowers High Courts to punish contempt of subordinate
courts, ensuring the smooth functioning of lower judiciary
Criticism:
1. Chilling Effect on Speech: Fear of contempt leads to self-censorship among journalists, activists, and
legal academics.
2. Against Right to dissent under Article 19 and 21.
3. Vague Definition: The term "scandalizing the court" is highly subjective and depends on the judge's
individual sensitivity.
4. Conflict of Interest: judiciary acts as the accuser, prosecutor, and the judge simultaneously violating the
fundamental principle of Natural Justice
5. Lack of Accountability: The judiciary's power to punish for contempt without adequate checks can lead
to arbitrary decisions..
6. Colonial Anachronism: The concept was abolished in the UK in 2013, yet India continues to use this
"monarchical" tool.
7. Inconsistent Punishment: The lack of a standardized sentencing policy leads to disparities in penalties
for similar offenses.
8. Obsolete "Majesty" Concept: In a modern democracy, institutional respect should be earned through
performance, not enforced by fear.

9. Subjective "Truth" Defense: Even with the 2006 Amendment, the burden of proving "bona fide intent"
remains prohibitively difficult for whistleblowers.
Way Forward:
1. Abolish "Scandalizing the Court": Follow the UK's Crime and Courts Act 2013 and limit criminal
contempt to "obstruction of justice" only.
2. The "Clear and Present Danger" Test: Adopt the US standard, where contempt is only invoked if the
speech poses an immediate threat to a fair trial.
3. Codifying "Fair Criticism": Explicitly define what constitutes academic, journalistic, or legal critique to
provide a "Safe Harbor" for citizens.
4. Ensure that contempt cases are resolved within 6 months.
5. Mandatory Mediation before punitive action for Civil Contempt
6. Create an independent committee to assist the Attorney General in deciding contempt permissions to
ensure non-partisanship.
7. Strengthening the Judicial Standards and Accountability framework can reduce the need for "defensive"
contempt laws.
Sealed cover jurisprudence
It refers to the practice where the executive (government) submits sensitive information to the judiciary in
a sealed envelope, accessible only to the judges and not to the opposing party.
Recent News
1. Following the full implementation of the MediaOne guidelines, courts have replaced "Sealed Covers"
with Public Interest Immunity (PII) claims, where a redacted summary of the evidence must be shared
with the petitioner.
2. The Apex Court recently reprimanded the Enforcement Directorate for "routinely" handing over case
diaries in sealed covers during bail hearings, calling it a violation of Article 21.
Major Cases
1. Pegasus Spyware Case (2021): The SC refused to accept a "limited affidavit" in a sealed cover from the
Centre
2. Rafale Fighter Jet Deal: accepted pricing details in sealed cover citing the Official Secrets Act.
3. Bhima Koregaon Case accepted evidence in sealed covers to deny bail to activists.
4. BCCI Reforms Case: The Mudgal Committee submitted names of cricketers suspected of match-fixing in
a sealed cover to protect their reputations during the probe.
5. INX Media Case (2019): The SC criticized the Delhi High Court for denying bail to P. Chidambaram based
solely on documents produced by the ED in a sealed cover.
Justification of Sealed Cover Jurisprudence
1. Protecting National Security: Safeguards classified military or intelligence data
2. Investigation Integrity: Prevents the "tipping off" of suspects or the destruction of evidence
3. Privacy of Individuals: Protects the reputation and dignity of persons
4. Protecting Identity of Informants
5. Diplomatic Sensitivity: Eg. Terms of sovereign guarantees in international defense contracts
6. Economic Stability: Eg. Data regarding distressed assets in major banks
7. Protection of Victims in sensitive cases like POCSO

8. Complying with Official Secrets Act & Section 123 of the Evidence Act
Criticism of Sealed Cover Jurisprudence
1. Violation of Natural Justice: Violates the "Right to be Heard" (Audi Alteram Partem)
2. Lack of Transparency: violates "justice must be seen to be done" principle
3. There is no codified law for its use, leaving it to the "ad-hoc" discretion of individual judges.
4. Erosion of Judicial Reasoning
5. The 2025 Media Freedom Index cited sealed covers as a major threat to independent journalism in India.
6. Interference with Fair Trial: withholding of evidence from the accused.
7. Undermining Accountability of executive. Eg. pegasus case
8. Democratic Decay
Way Forward
1. Appointment of Amicus Curiae: appoint an independent lawyer to "see" the sealed cover and argue on
behalf of the absent party.
2. Redacted Disclosures: Mandate the state to provide "Redacted Summaries" that remove sensitive names
but keep the "gist" of the allegations clear.
3. Amend the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 to define strict, narrow categories where sealed covers are
permissible.
4. The Proportionality Test: Apply the Puttaswamy (2017) test to ensure that "secrecy" is the least
restrictive measure possible to achieve the goal.
5. In-Camera Hearings
Judicial Recusal in India
In Delhi Liquor Policy Case a recusal plea was raised against Justice Swarna Kanta Sharma citing perceived
ideological bias.
Judicial Recusal is the act of a judge voluntarily abstaining from participating in a legal proceeding because
of a conflict of interest or a reasonable apprehension that they cannot remain impartial.
It flows from two foundational maxims of law:
1. Nemo judex in causa sua - "No one shall be a judge in their own cause"
2. Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done
Provisions and Procedures in India
1. No Codified Law: Unlike the US (28 U.S. Code § 455), India has no statutory law governing recusal. It is
governed by judicial conventions and precedents.
2. Restatement of Values of Judicial Life - forbids a judge from deciding a case where they hold a
pecuniary interest, unless the concerned parties have no objections. It is non-binding.
3. Constitutional Oath: Derived from the Third Schedule, where a judge swears to perform duties "without
fear or favour, affection or ill-will."
4. Two Types:
a. Automatic (Sua Sponte): The judge withdraws voluntarily upon identifying a conflict.
b. Requested: A litigant files a plea for recusal. Final decision rests with the judge.
5. Reassignment: Once a judge recuses, the case is sent to the Chief Justice (Master of Roster) for
assignment to a different bench.
196

### [Smash Mains Source Page 195](pages/mains/mains_page_195.pdf)

6. The Doctrine of Necessity is an exception. It says that a judge may still hear a matter despite a potential
conflict if there is no alternative forum or judge available
Grounds for Recusal
1. Personal or prior professional association with a party
2. Earlier involvement as lawyer or judge in the same matter
3. Financial interest in the case outcome
4. Engagement in ex parte (private) communications related to the case
Justification of Recusal
1. Preservation of Public Confidence in impartiality of Judiciary
2. Preventing Prejudgment - Prior Advocacy Conflict - Eg. Justice U.U. Lalit recused from the Ram
Janmabhoomi dispute as he had previously appeared as an advocate in a related matter
3. Protection Institutional Integrity in Politically Sensitive Cases - Eg. CJI Sanjiv Khanna and CJI Surya
Kant both recused from petitions challenging the CEC appointment law
4. Upholding Due Process: Article 21's "Right to a Fair Trial" implicitly requires an impartial adjudicator for
every citizen.
5. Upholds judge's oath to act "without fear or favour, affection or ill-will" under Schedule III
6. Aligns India with international norms like Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct (2002).
7. A judge who has pre-judged a legal or factual issue must not decide the same matter again.
Limitations and Challenges in Recusal
1. No Codified Law - based on the conscience of judges, leading to opacity.
2. Bench Hunting/Forum Shopping: Litigants can request recusal of "tough" judges to get a more favorable
bench assigned.
3. Master of Roster Paradox - A recused CJI cannot adjudicate the case but retains roster control to decide
who hears it
4. Lack of Transparency: Most judges recuse without providing written reasons
5. Sudden recusal after a few hearings forces a "de-novo" (fresh) hearing, wasting judicial time.
6. Subjectivity of "Conscience": Since it's a personal decision, two judges may treat the same conflict
differently, causing inconsistency.
7. Strategic use of recusal petitions by litigants to stall execution of orders or final hearings.
8. Absence of Review Mechanism: There is no legal way to challenge a judge's refusal to recuse except via a
review petition later.
Major SC Judgments
1. Manak Lal v. Dr. Prem Chand (1957): Established the "Real Likelihood of Bias" test.
2. Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India (1987): Held that the test is the "Reasonableness of apprehension" in the
mind of the party. (not actual bias)
3. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (2015): Clarified that pecuniary interest makes
recusal automatic.
4. Indore Development Authority Case (2019): Ruled that a judge is not disqualified from a larger bench
just for passing an earlier smaller-bench order.
Way Forward
1. Mandatory Disclosure: Judges should provide a written reason for recusal to ensure transparency
2. Codify Recusal Standards Under Article 145 or by Statute
197

---

### [Smash Mains Source Page 196](pages/mains/mains_page_196.pdf)

3. Pre-Hearing Disclosure: Conflicts should be disclosed at the "admission stage" to prevent delays during
final hearings.
4. Adopting the UK's "Fair-minded and Informed Observer" test (Porter v. Magill) for a more objective
standard.
5. Review by a Larger Bench: In sensitive cases, a recusal request could be decided by a 3-judge bench
instead of the concerned judge alone.
6. Penalty for using recusal as a tool for "bench hunting."
Post-retirement appointments of judges
1. In 2024, hours after resigning as a judge of the Calcutta HC, joined a political party and contested 2024
LS elections.
2. Justice B.R. Gavai publicly pledged to refuse any post-retirement appointment from the government,
arguing it is essential to maintain public confidence.
- Since 1950, over 40 CJIs have accepted post-retirement positions in various capacities.
- Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy found that nearly 72% of retired SC judges take up official assignments
(Tribunals, Commissions, or Governorships) within 2 years of retirement.
- Over 40 Central Acts specifically require a retired SC or HC judge to head bodies like the NHRC, NGT,
and NCDRC.
Constitutional Provisions:
1. Article 124(7): Former Supreme Court judges cannot practice law in any Indian court or authority.
2. Article 220: Retired High Court judges are prohibited from acting in any court except the Supreme Court
and other High Courts.
Benefits of Post-Retirement Appointments
1. Utilization of Expertise - as per Former CJI D.Y. Chandrachud, the "vast experience" of judges is a
valuable national resource that shouldn't be entirely discarded.
2. Statutory Compliance: Eg. Protection of Human Rights Act requires a former CJI or SC judge to lead the
NHRC.
3. Judicial Continuity in Tribunals: Judges are better equipped than bureaucrats to handle "judicial
functions" like cross-examination and evidence.
4. Retired judges act as neutral and "trusted" members for heading sensitive inquiry commissions. Eg.
Justice J.S. Verma Committee after the Nirbhaya case.
5. Institutional Memory: Long-serving judges help maintain consistency in how specialized laws (like the
IBC) are interpreted across the country.
6. Standardizing Quasi-Judicial Work: Judges bring a "standardized template" for writing judgments to
administrative bodies that might otherwise be arbitrary.
7. Filling Vacancy Gaps: They serve as a ready pool of "ad-hoc" members for temporary commissions,
saving the time required for fresh recruitments. Eg. Delimitation Commissions
Criticism:
1. Erosion of Judicial Independence: The "hope" for a future job may subconsciously influence a judge's
rulings in favor of the government.
2. Public Perception Crisis: Eg. nomination of a former CJI to the Rajya Sabha (2020)
